column2: These do their works ever in rivalry with one another and accomplish their aims, telling each other.
And you should fear your kinsmen as one fears death always; a kinsman does not tolerate a royal sage, like a rival king.
No one but a kinsman, mighty-armed, welcomes the ruin of an upright, gentle, generous, modest and truthful man.
To be without kinsmen is not very pleasant, and kinsmen are not to be disregarded; others scorn a man who has no kinsmen.
For one wronged by other men, a kinsman is the refuge; a kinsman never tolerates the wrong done to his kinsman by others.
One knows oneself to be wronged even by relatives; they have virtues and in them lack of virtues too is seen.
A non-kinsman does not favour, nor a non-kinsman cast aside the smeared; both are seen in the world of kin, the good and the bad.
One should honour and worship them always in word and deed, do what is pleasing to them and do nothing unpleasant to them.
One should always behave toward them as if trusting though not trusting; for neither fault nor merit is seen in them untouched.
For a man so behaving and careful, enemies become pleased and even become friends.
One who always behaves so in the circle of kin and relatives, among friends, enemies and in lordship, stays long in fame."

Here too they recite this ancient history, the dialogue of Vasudeva with the divine sage Narada.
mahabharata:12:82.3	A supreme counsel is not to be known by one who is not a friend, Narada, nor by an unlearned person, nor by a friend who is learned but not self-possessed.
Relying on your friendship I shall say something to you, Narada, and, having considered all my mind, I ask you, who go to heaven.
I serve my kinsmen in a servant's role under the name of lordship; I am an eater of half the enjoyments and endure harsh words.
As one wishing fire churns the fire-stick, so a harsh word, divine sage, churns my heart; that burns me always.
In Sankarshana there is strength always, in Gada delicacy, and Pradyumna is mad with beauty; I am helpless, Narada.
Others, the Andhakas and Vrishnis, are very fortunate, strong and hard to approach, endowed with constant exertion, Narada.
He for whom they are not is not, and he for whom they are has only hardship; restrained always by the two, I choose neither one."

This calamity within you, Krishna, born of your own deeds—Akrura, Bhoja and their lines, all these are their descendants.
mahabharata:12:82.15	The lordship obtained by you for wealth or desire or through a door of disgust was handed over elsewhere.
mahabharata:12:82.16	Now that it has taken root and the word of birth has become allied, it cannot be taken back by you, like vomited food.
mahabharata:12:82.17	The kingdom of Babhru and Ugrasena cannot be obtained in any way, Krishna, for fear of division among kin, and by you especially.
mahabharata:12:82.18	If that were accomplished with effort by doing a very hard deed, it would be a great loss and expense, or it would be destruction again.
mahabharata:12:82.19	With a non-iron, gentle weapon that cuts the heart, draw out the tongue of all, wiping and wiping away.
What is this non-iron, gentle weapon, sage, by which I may draw out their tongues, wiping and wiping away?

Giving food according to ability constantly, patience, self-control, uprightness, and honour as is fitting—this is the non-iron weapon.
mahabharata:12:82.22	Of kinsmen who wish to speak bitter and light words, calm their hearts, speech and minds with your speech.
mahabharata:12:82.23	No one who is not a great man, not self-possessed, and without helpers takes up a great burden; having taken it, bear it with your chest.
mahabharata:12:82.24	All draw heavy loads; an ox draws on level ground; on a hard road a good-natured bull carries the hard-to-bear load.
mahabharata:12:82.25	Assemblies are ruined by division; you, Keshava, are chief of the assembly; so act that this assembly does not perish, having got you.
mahabharata:12:82.26	A clever man does not keep an assembly together except by understanding and patience, by restraint of the senses, and by giving up wealth.
mahabharata:12:82.27	Blessed, famous, life-giving and good is the increase of one's own side; do so, Krishna, that the kin may not perish.
mahabharata:12:82.28	Nothing is unknown to you, lord, of the future and present; by the rule of the six measures and the rules of marching.
mahabharata:12:82.29	Madhavas, Kukuras, Bhojas, and all the Andhakas and Vrishnis are attached to you, mighty-armed one, and the worlds and the lords of worlds.
mahabharata:12:82.30	The sages also wait on your wisdom, Madhava; you are the teacher of all beings and know their coming and going; reaching you, best of the Yadus, the kin prosper in happiness.

One who tells of the royal treasury being carried off by a minister, whether he is paid or unpaid, Yudhishthira,
mahabharata:12:83.3	is to be heard in private, and that minister is to be guarded against; for the ministers mostly kill the informer, Bharata.
mahabharata:12:83.4	Those who plunder the royal treasury all combine and oppress the protector of the royal treasury; he perishes unprotected.
mahabharata:12:83.5	Here too they recite this ancient history, what the sage Kalakavrikshiya said to the Kosala king.
mahabharata:12:83.6	When Kshemadarshin had attained lordship over the Kosalas, the sage Kalakavrikshiya came, we have heard.
mahabharata:12:83.7	Having caged a crow, he first went about the country of Kshemadarshin, attentive, seeking his aim again and again.
mahabharata:12:83.8	I study the science of crows; crows tell me the future, the past and the present."
So going about the kingdom with various men, he asked about the misdeeds of all the king's officers.
This one and that one know that you have stolen the royal treasury, thus the crow says; let that be quickly followed.
He also told of other plunderers of the royal treasury, and no word of his was ever heard to be unfulfilled.
All the king's officers, wronged by him, delight of the Kurus, struck the crow at night while the sage slept, passing him by.
Seeing the crow pierced by an arrow in the cage, in the forenoon the Brahmana said to Kshemadarshin:

King, I ask safety of you, the lord and master of life and wealth; permitted by you I would speak a word to you, with your priest.
mahabharata:12:83.18	Tormented for a friend, devoted with my whole self, I take your aim, I who say it patiently.
mahabharata:12:83.19	Wishing to awaken a friend like a charioteer a good horse, one very impelled by anger, bringing a beneficial reason.
mahabharata:12:83.20	Such a friend should be forgiven by one who understands, ever wishing lordship and prosperity.
The king replied to him: "Whatever you may say to me, why should I not forgive, wishing my own good?
Brahmana, promise, speak if you wish; whatever you tell me, I will do, Brahmana.
Knowing policy and its failings and the fears from your servants, to explain the livelihood with devotion; your coming is not out of place.
This fault was told earlier by teachers, king: the lot of servants is a lack of refuge, the livelihood of living with a king.
They say that one who consorts with kings is among venomous snakes; kings have many friends and have many friends likewise.
From all of them, they say, there is fear for those who serve kings; and from one of them alone, O king, fear may arise in a moment.
Absolute carelessness cannot be avoided by a lord of the earth, but carelessness must never be committed by one who wishes prosperity.
A king stumbles from carelessness, and in his stumbling there is no life; one instructed should approach a king like a blazing fire.
A man should wait on his lord, master of life and wealth, like an enraged venomous snake, with care, thinking "I am nobody."
Fearing ill speech, ill deed, ill position, ill sitting, ill going, signal and bodily gesture,
a king pleased fulfils all aims like a deity; enraged he burns even the root like Vaishvanara. Thus Maya spoke, king, and so it proceeds.
Then I shall do more and more; a minister like us gives help of wisdom in calamity.
The crow was aimed at me for death, king; I do not blame you here nor those whose beloved you are; know the beneficial and harmful, and do not be of distant mind.
Those who live in your house intent on taking, wishing ill for beings, I was aimed at by such.
Those who wish the kingdom immediately upon your destruction succeed only by contriving with insiders, O king.
Fearing them, O king, I shall go to another hermitage; for an arrow was fitted by them and fell on the crow, lord.
By trickery my crow was sent to Yama's abode; I have seen this with the long eye of austerity, king.
With a crow as hook I have crossed this river for you, with many crocodiles, fish and crocodile-like monsters, full of timis and timingila whales,
with stationary rocks and thorns, thronged with tigers, lions and elephants, hard to approach and enter, like a Himalayan cave.
A fort of darkness is reached by fire, and a water-fort by boats; for descending into a king's fort the wise know no remedy.
Your kingdom is dense, covered in darkness; one cannot trust here even you, how much less me?
Therefore this is not a good dwelling where good and bad are held equal; here there is only killing for good and evil deeds alike, without doubt.
By justice, punishment is for the evil deed; how can there be killing for the good deed? It is not right to stay long here; the wise should go quickly.
The Sita river, O king, is one in which a raft sinks; I consider this net killing all like that.
You are honey-hot, food mixed with poison; your nature is like that of the wicked, not of the good; you are like a well surrounded by venomous snakes.
As a river with fort-like ghats, high banks, with karira and cane, of sweet water, so are you; you are like a royal swan with dogs, vultures and jackals.
As a great thicket grows relying on a great tree and then covers it and grows beyond it,
by that very means a fierce forest fire with fuel burns; such are your ministers, O king; purify them.
They were made by you, protected by you, and having slighted you, they wish to kill you, who are dear to you.
Dwelling here with suspicion and guarding against carelessness, like a snake inside the house, hero, like a wife in her own home, testing the character of the king and those living with him.
Is the king self-controlled? Are the inner ones conquered? Is the king dear to them? Are the subjects dear to the king?
I came here wishing to test, best of kings; you please me, king, like food to a hungry man.
Your ministers do not please me, like water to the thirstless; the fault against me was made by them with "He does the king's work"; there is no other reason, I have no doubt.
I have no grudge against them; that went to them as their fault; one fears an enemy badly struck, like a snake with a broken back.
Honoured with more retinue and more hospitality, best of Brahmanas, dwell again in my house.
Those who do not wish you, Brahmana, will not live in my house; you alone must know what to do next.
Consider how punishment may be for the evil done and how the good deed is done, revered one, and appoint me to the good.
Without showing this fault, make each one weak; then, knowing the reason, strike man by man.
Many with one fault might crush even thorns; for fear of the leak of counsel, king, I say this to you.
We Brahmanas are mild in punishment, with a trace of pity; I wish you well and others too as myself.
King, I declare myself: I am related to you, the sage named Kalakavrikshiya.
A friend of your father, approved, true to my word, when your kingdom was in calamity and your father had died, king,
I gave up all desires and practised austerity; out of affection I say this to you, that you may not err again.
Having seen both sorrow and joy, having obtained the kingdom by chance, how can you be careless with a kingdom resting on ministers?"
Then there was great rejoicing in the royal house and in the house of the priest, best of Brahmanas.
The sage Kalakavrikshiya, having made the earth under one umbrella for the renowned Kosala, sacrificed with the best sacrifices.
Hearing that beneficial word, the Kosala king ruled the earth, and the king did as he was told, Bharata."

Very prosperous, very brave, learned Brahmanas, well content and of great exertion in works, son of Kunti,
mahabharata:12:84.3	these helpers you should wish for in all calamities, Bharata; a man of good family, honoured always, does not hide his strength.
mahabharata:12:84.4	Pleased or displeased, pained or robbed, he turns it back mostly; that one alone protected.
mahabharata:12:84.5	Of good family, born in the country, wise, handsome, learned, bold and devoted, these should be your retinue.
mahabharata:12:84.6	Those of bad family and the greedy, cruel and shameless attend you, dear one, only as long as their hands are half-full.
mahabharata:12:84.7	With wealth, honour, gifts and hospitality, and various enjoyments, those you think sharers in wealth will be sharers in happiness.
mahabharata:12:84.8	Those of unbroken conduct, learned, of good conduct and observed vows, not petty, truthful, would not abandon you though always seeking.
mahabharata:12:84.9	The ignoble who do not know the agreement, the dull-minded, you should be wary of, and know them to have lapsed from agreement.
mahabharata:12:84.12	One who honours the able and does not vie with those not to be vied with, and who would not abandon dharma from desire, fear, anger or greed,
mahabharata:12:84.13	not proud, truthful, able, self-conquered, honouring the worthy, should be your helper in counsel, tested in every condition.
mahabharata:12:84.14	Of good family, endowed with truth, patient, skilled, self-possessed, brave, grateful and truthful: these are marks of the best, Partha.
mahabharata:12:84.15	For such a man so behaving, who knows, enemies become pleased and then become friends.
mahabharata:12:84.16	After this a king, restrained, of trained understanding and wishing prosperity, should test the merits and faults of his ministers.
mahabharata:12:84.17	Connected with trustworthy men of good birth born in his own country, not capable of being bribed, not unfaithful, well tested from every side,
mahabharata:12:84.18	warriors, hereditary, and others also should be made, by a man wishing prosperity.
mahabharata:12:84.19	Those whose training in discipline is natural and good, with energy, steadiness, patience, purity, loyalty, steadfastness and firmness,
mahabharata:12:84.20	tested in merits, ever of mature mind, bearers of the burden, who have passed the five tests, should a king make workers for his aims.
mahabharata:12:84.21	Of sufficient speech, heroes, skilled in understanding, of good family, endowed with truth, who know signs, not harsh,
mahabharata:12:84.22	who know arrangements of place and time, wishing the good of their master's work, a king should make ministers in all affairs always.
mahabharata:12:84.23	One of reduced energy and not glad never resolves; he necessarily gives rise to doubts in all works.
mahabharata:12:84.24	Likewise a minister of little learning, even of noble birth, joined to dharma, wealth and desire, is not fit to test counsel.
mahabharata:12:84.25	Likewise one of low birth, though very learned, is bewildered in matters to be inferred, like a blind man without a leader.
mahabharata:12:84.26	One of unsteady resolve, though intelligent and learned, and knowing means, is not fit to carry on work for long.
mahabharata:12:84.27	From mere conduct alone no examination of particulars arises for an unlearned, ill-minded man in the work.
mahabharata:12:84.28	There is no trust in a minister who is not devoted; therefore counsel should not be revealed to one not devoted.
mahabharata:12:84.29	An insincere one, joined with ministers, would trouble a king, entering like fire a tree through the holes made by the wind.
mahabharata:12:84.30	Sometimes the master is angry and removes from position, in rage he abuses, and afterward is pleased.
mahabharata:12:84.31	Those things can be borne by one who is devoted; the anger of ministers is like a thunderbolt's crash.
mahabharata:12:84.32	One who bears them out of wish to please his master, sharing equal joy and sorrow, such a man should be consulted in affairs.
mahabharata:12:84.33	But a crooked one, though devoted and endowed with other qualities and wisdom, is not fit to hear the king's counsel.
mahabharata:12:84.34	A friend who is connected with enemies and does not honour the townsfolk is not fit to hear the king's counsel.
mahabharata:12:84.35	An unlearned, impure, stiff friend who serves enemies, boasts, is angry and greedy is not fit to hear counsel.
mahabharata:12:84.36	A newcomer, though devoted and very learned, honoured or shared with, is not fit to hear counsel.
mahabharata:12:84.37	One who has once been accused even for a small matter, though joined to other merits, is not fit to hear counsel.
mahabharata:12:84.38	One of trained mind, intelligent, wise, a countryman, pure, clean in all works, is fit to hear counsel.
mahabharata:12:84.39	One endowed with knowledge and discernment, who knows his own and others' natures, a friend equal to the king himself, is fit to hear counsel.
mahabharata:12:84.40	Truthful, endowed with good conduct, deep, modest, gentle, one whose father and grandfather were such, is fit to hear counsel.
mahabharata:12:84.41	Content, esteemed, true, brave, hating evil, knowing counsel and time, valiant, is fit to hear counsel.
mahabharata:12:84.42	One who can bring all the world under his sway by conciliation—to him counsel should be applied by one who wishes to use the rod, O king.
mahabharata:12:84.43	One in whom townsfolk and country folk have placed trust by dharma, a warrior and wise in policy, is fit to hear counsel.
mahabharata:12:84.44	Therefore ministers endowed with all these qualities, well honoured, knowing natures, should be at least three, wishing greatness.
mahabharata:12:84.45	The ministers should mark the weak points in their own natures and the enemy's, for the king's kingdom grows rooted in counsel.
mahabharata:12:84.46	An enemy should not see his weak point, but he should find the enemy's weak points; he should hide like a tortoise its limbs and guard his own opening.
mahabharata:12:84.47	Ministers who are wise are the seizers of counsel of a kingdom; a king is the combiner of counsel, and the rest of the people are its limbs.
mahabharata:12:84.48	They call the kingdom rooted in stationed agents and counsel its essence; ministers here follow the master for livelihood.
mahabharata:12:84.49	Having cast off pride and anger, conceit and jealousy, content, he should always take counsel with ministers who have passed the five tests.
mahabharata:12:84.50	Having fixed his mind on their varied deliberations, he should understand it, and report his own decision and the other's decision at the time of final counsel.
mahabharata:12:84.51	Approaching a Brahmana teacher who knows dharma, wealth and desire, he should ask about the highest aim; when a conclusion is made with him, he should lead that course without attachment.
mahabharata:12:84.52	Thus counsel should always be taken, say those who know the truth and certainty of counsel; therefore you should always lead counsel able to win over the subjects.
mahabharata:12:84.53	No dwarf, hunchback, thin man or lame man, no blind, dull, woman or eunuch, and no animal should move about, in front, behind, above or below.
mahabharata:12:84.54	Ascending an empty window, on an open spot without kusha and kasha grass, avoiding faults of speech and body, he should consult on the matter in good time.
What is the one word, Brahmana, by which a man acting rightly would obtain the standard of all beings and great fame?

Conciliation is the one word, Shakra, by which a man acting rightly would obtain the standard of all beings and great fame.
mahabharata:12:85.4	This one word, Shakra, bringing happiness to all the world, acted on toward all beings, makes one always dear.
mahabharata:12:85.5	He who never speaks, ever with frowning face, becomes hated by beings, not practising conciliation here.
mahabharata:12:85.6	One who looks first and speaks first, and speaks first with a smile, makes the world well disposed.
mahabharata:12:85.7	Even a gift, unaccompanied by conciliation, does not please beings anywhere, like seasonless food.
mahabharata:12:85.8	Even a non-giver, Shakra, speaking sweet speech, brings this whole world under his sway by conciliation.
mahabharata:12:85.9	Therefore conciliation should be practised by those who wish to use the rod here; it brings fruit, and people are not troubled by him.
Thus told, Shakra did all with his priest; so you too, son of Kunti, practise this rightly.

A king devoted to protecting the subjects by pure dealing, having obtained dharma and fame, wins both worlds, pure.
mahabharata:12:86.3	What kind of dealing and with whom should a king deal? Asked this, greatly wise one, you ought to tell as it is.
These qualities said earlier are for a man; I think they do not exist in a single man.
It is as you say, greatly wise and intelligent one; a man joined to these many qualities is hard to find.
But in brief, character is not hard to find with effort; I shall tell what kind of ministers you should make.
Four learned, bold, sattvic, pure Brahmanas, and three pure, trained Shudras for earlier work,
and a Sūta endowed with eight qualities, a bard of the Puranas, fifty years of age, bold, without envy,
endowed with intelligence and memory, trained, looking equally on disputants in a case, able, not greedy for wealth, should be employed.
And a secret matter of yours should not be taken up where it would hurt the matter; if the matter fails, that unrighteousness would afflict you and them.
Your kingdom would scatter like flocks of birds from a hawk, and would constantly leak like a shattered ship on the sea.
For a king who protects subjects wrongly by unrighteousness, fear arises within, and his heaven is obstructed."
What this one did, Arjunaka, is the cause urging us; the cause of his destruction is none other; he is slain by his own deed.
Devoted to the dharma of giving, ever pleasant of speech, the eldest of them, Khaninetra, oppressed them all.
Overcome by affection for my son, I was told what was good by the wise—by Vidura, Bhishma, Drona and Kripa.
Thus told by Yuyudhana, Pradyumna, best of chariot-warriors, honoured his word and scorned Hardikya.
Seeing his brothers fallen, Yudhishthira, king of dharma, afflicted with grief, said to the thousand-eyed (Indra):
Hearing those voices, matching that place, the king reflected: "What is this, brought about by fate?"
